chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: For interval sessions and speed work, nothing replaces a measured track. The main athletics venues in Mauritius are the Maryse Justin Stadium in Réduit and the Stade Germain Comarmond in Bambous.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: The stadium is named after Maryse Justin-Pyndiah, a Mauritian long-distance runner who specialised in the marathon. It is used by the Mauritius Athletics Association and hosts national championships.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: In the west, near Bambous, this stadium is used mostly for football and athletics, and has also hosted national youth athletics championships.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: Public opening hours and fees for casual runners are not published by the athletics association, whose calendars list competitions and club training.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: The reliable way to train on a track is to join an athletics club or to ask the Mauritius Athletics Association or the stadium administration about access.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: Runners doing structured speed work, such as 400 m repeats or tempo intervals, and anyone preparing for road races who wants precise pacing.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: For an open-access measured loop without traffic, the Trou aux Cerfs crater rim in Curepipe is the usual alternative.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text: Black River Gorges National Park protects the largest area of native forest left in Mauritius, in the south-west of the island. It is home to rare endemic birds such as the echo parakeet, the pink pigeon and the Mauritius kestrel.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Entry to the park and its trails is free.
There are two official entrances with visitor centres: Pétrin, on the plateau, and Rivière Noire, at the bottom of the gorges on the west side.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text: Rangers there can advise on current trail conditions, and trail maps are available. Some sources say the park gates close at about 5 pm.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text: The Macchabée forest loop starts from Pétrin and runs through some of the best native forest on the island. Its length varies by variant, with sources quoting anywhere from about 8 to 14 km.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text: The Parakeet Trail is a much harder one-way descent of roughly 6 to 8 km through steep, technical terrain, taking most people three to four hours.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Gentler options include short walks to viewpoints such as Alexandra Falls and the Black River Gorges viewpoint.
Difficulty ranges from easy viewpoint strolls to hard, technical descents.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text: Difficulty ranges from easy viewpoint strolls to hard, technical descents. Trails are not always well marked, so check the route and conditions at a visitor centre before you set off.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text: May to November is the best season, with fewer muddy paths. The plateau is often misty and cooler than the coast, so bring a light rain jacket.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: Black River Peak, Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire, is the highest point in Mauritius at about 828 m.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: It stands inside Black River Gorges National Park, and despite being the highest summit it is one of the shortest hikes to a major peak on the island.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: The usual trailhead is on the B103 Plaine Champagne road, close to the Black River Gorges viewpoint.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: Parking at the trailhead fits only two or three cars, so many hikers leave the car at the viewpoint car park a short walk away.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: From the viewpoint side the return hike is about 3 to 3.5 km with under 200 m of climbing, and most people reach the top in about an hour to an hour and a half.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: The trail is mostly well maintained and easy to follow through native forest. The final section is steeper and rockier, and ropes help on the rock in places.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:
The trailhead is not well signposted, so check a map before you go. From the summit you look down over the west coast, Tamarin bay and Le Morne.
May to November is drier and less muddy.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:
May to November is drier and less muddy. Start in the morning, and turn back if the summit is in cloud and the rock is wet.
Entry to the national park is free and no permit is required.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: Guided hikes are available if you prefer not to navigate the unsigned start. Bring a light jacket: Plaine Champagne is noticeably cooler and windier than the coast.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text: Bras d'Eau National Park is a coastal forest park in the north-east of Mauritius. Its trails run through forest that includes mangroves and endemic trees, and they are much flatter than the mountain trails of the west and centre.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text: Bras d'Eau is a good place for fairly easy trail running.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text: Trails start from the visitor centre, and the gentle terrain makes it a natural first step from road running to trail running, or a place for relaxed long runs on soft ground.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text: Beginners trying trail running for the first time, runners in the east and north of the island, and anyone who wants shaded, quiet running away from traffic without technical terrain.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text: Being on the coast, it is warm and humid; the forest gives more shade than beach routes. After heavy rain, parts of the trails can be muddy.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text:
After heavy rain, parts of the trails can be muddy.
Pick up information at the visitor centre before heading out, and stay on the marked trails to protect the forest.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text: When the goal is easy mileage, recovery runs or speed on the flat, the coast is the place to train. Each side of the island has its own classic route.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text: Each side of the island has its own classic route.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text: Flic en Flac has about 8 km of white-sand beach and a flat seafront road, which makes it one of the best places on the island for beginners and for early-morning runs.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text:
Running on sand also builds strength in the feet and calves.
Belle Mare has a beachfront path and roughly 1.5 km of firm sand road along the beach, with quiet farm roads inland for longer runs.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
sections: North: Mont Choisy and Grand Baie
chunks.text:
One mapped beachfront loop from Belle Mare is about 10 km.
The coastal road leading to Mont Choisy beach is quieter than the main roads.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
sections: North: Mont Choisy and Grand Baie
chunks.text: Sections of the B13 through Pereybère, Grand Baie and Mont Choisy have a narrow sidewalk or shoulder, so run there with care and at quiet times.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text:
A flat trail runs along the water at Le Morne, a scenic option for an easy run before or after hiking the mountain.
The coast is hot and humid for most of the year.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text: Run at dawn or late in the day, carry water, and wear shoes on rocky beaches where sea urchins hide.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text: Corps de Garde is a mountain of about 720 m that towers over Rose Hill, Beau Bassin and Quatre Bornes. From its ridge you see the whole central plateau, the west coast and, on clear days, Port Louis.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text: The classic route is a loop above Rose Hill. One detailed guide describes it as about 7 km with more than 600 m of ascent, and other sources give 2 to 4 hours.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text:
The path is marked with white stones up to the ridge.
It is not really a beginner hike. The climb starts steeply, with rocky steps where you need your hands, and the slopes near the summit are challenging.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text:
Sources rate it medium to hard.
The route has very little shade, so avoid the middle of the day. May to November is cooler; in summer, go at first light.
It is free and no guide is needed.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text: It is free and no guide is needed. Take about two litres of water per person, sun protection and shoes with good grip.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text: Black River Gorges National Park is the main trail-running training ground in Mauritius. It has about 60 km of trails, many of them hilly with challenging, technical footing, through native forest between the Pétrin plateau and the Rivière Noire entrance.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text: The park is where you train for real mountain races. Long runs on the forest loops build endurance, and the climbs out of the gorges build strength for steep ascents and technical descents.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text: The Royal Raid, the island's longest-running trail race, held since 2006, takes place in the Black River Gorges, with distances such as 15 km, 37 km and 70 km offered in past editions.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text:
Training on its trails is the most race-specific preparation you can do on the island.
Intermediate and experienced trail runners preparing for the Royal Raid, the Dodo Trail or races abroad.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text:
Beginners should start on the shorter, well-used trails from the Pétrin visitor centre and run with someone who knows the network.
Footing gets very muddy and slippery in the wet season.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text: Footing gets very muddy and slippery in the wet season. The austral winter, from May to November, is the best period for long runs. Trails are not always well marked, and there is little phone signal in places.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text: Entry is free. Check routes with rangers at the visitor centres, carry water and a map, and tell someone your planned route.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text: La Tourelle de Tamarin is a steep mountain less than a kilometre from the coast at Tamarin, on the west of the island.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text:
Runners use it as a brutal hill-training ground: about 560 m of ascent over roughly 4.4 km return.
This is a place for vertical training, not for setting times.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text: Repeats on the steepest part build the climbing strength needed for mountain races. Fixed ropes equip some of the steps, so expect to use your hands.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text:
The descent is as important to practise as the climb: take it carefully, especially when tired.
Trail runners and hikers preparing for races with a lot of climbing, such as the Dodo Trail or the Royal Raid.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text:
It is not a beginner route; build up on easier hills first, such as Le Pouce or the Port Louis hills.
The west coast is hot and dry, and the slope offers little shade.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text: Train at dawn or late in the afternoon. Darkness falls quickly in Mauritius, in about twenty minutes, between about 5:45 pm and 7 pm depending on the season, so carry a headlamp on evening sessions.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text: Bring plenty of water and gloves for the rope sections. Avoid it after rain, when the steps become slippery.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text: Le Morne Brabant is the 556 m basalt mountain on the south-western peninsula of Mauritius.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text: It is a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, inscribed in 2008, because its cliffs sheltered escaped enslaved people, the maroons, in the 18th and 19th centuries. Hike it with that history in mind.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text:
Hike it with that history in mind.
The trail starts at a gate near the base of the mountain, where hikers sign in and out of a register for safety.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text: The lower trail climbs to a viewpoint with a large cross, with views over the lagoon and the south-west coast. Above the cross, the final section to the summit is a steep scramble where you climb on all fours.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text:
A full return to the summit takes about 3 to 5 hours.
Published opening hours differ between sources, but the gate opens early in the morning and late starts are not allowed, with the last departure in the early afternoon.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text: Access is closed on rainy days. Sources also disagree on whether a licensed guide is required above the cross. Check the current rules on site or with a local operator before you plan the summit.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text:
To the cross, the hike is moderate but hot. The summit section is hard and exposed, and should be skipped after rain because the rock becomes slippery.
Start at dawn.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text: Start at dawn. There is very little shade, and the south-west coast gets hot by mid-morning. The cooler months from May to November are the most pleasant.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text: Le Pouce, "the thumb", is the third-highest mountain in Mauritius at about 812 m.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text: Its thumb-shaped summit rises from the Moka Range directly above Port Louis, and it is one of the most popular half-day hikes on the island because it is short, well trodden and close to the capital.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text: The best-known trailhead is the village of Petit Verger, near Saint Pierre, where a well-marked path climbs through sugar cane fields and patches of forest. Other approaches start from the Moka side and from the Tranquebar side of Port Louis.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text:
A common return route is about 4 to 5 km, and most walkers take 2 to 4 hours depending on the starting point and their pace.
The hike is easy to moderate for most of the way.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text: The last few hundred metres to the summit are steep and rocky, and you need good balance and sometimes your hands. The reward is a 360° view over Port Louis, the northern plains and the neighbouring peak of Pieter Both.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text:
The drier, cooler months from May to November are the most comfortable. Start early in the morning: the path has stretches without shade. After heavy rain the upper rock section becomes slippery.
No permit or guide is needed.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text: No permit or guide is needed. Carry at least a litre and a half of water, a hat and shoes with good grip. Guided sunrise and sunset hikes are also offered by local operators.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text: Lion Mountain, Montagne du Lion, rises to about 480 m above Vieux Grand Port, near Mahébourg on the south-east coast. Seen from the coast road, its ridge looks like a resting lion.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
It is the best-known hike in the east of the island.
The trail starts in Vieux Grand Port, near the police station, and crosses sugar cane fields before climbing the lion's spine.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
The return hike is about 4.5 to 5 km and usually takes 2 to 3 hours. From the top you look over the bay of Grand Port, the lagoon and the islets offshore.
Sources rate it moderate to hard.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text: Sources rate it moderate to hard. The first part of the climb follows a rocky spine where you use your hands as well as your legs, with a few easy but airy scrambling moves.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
Waymarking is limited to paint marks and ribbons, so a guide is advisable if you do not know the route.
Hike it in dry weather only, in any season. The rock becomes dangerous when wet.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
The rock becomes dangerous when wet. There is no water on the route and little shade, so an early morning start is best.
Carry all your water. Guided hikes with local guides are offered from Mahébourg and the surrounding area.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text: Pieter Both is the second-highest mountain in Mauritius, at about 820 m, in the Moka Range above Port Louis. It is instantly recognisable by the round boulder, the "head", balanced on top of its narrow summit spire.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text: A hiking path through forest and grassland leads to the shoulder below the head. The final section, up the head itself, is a rock climb rather than a hike.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text:
Guides use fixed ropes and metal rungs bolted into the basalt, and supply helmets, harnesses and ropes after a safety briefing. Allow a full day with a guided group.
This is the hardest summit in this collection.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text: This is the hardest summit in this collection. Local guides describe it as the only Mauritian ascent that genuinely requires guiding, and hikers who have done it warn that it is dangerous without a guide.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text:
A head for heights is essential, and it is not suitable for beginners.
Climb only in dry, calm weather, from May to November if possible.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text:
Wind and wet rock make the summit block unsafe, and guides cancel when conditions are poor.
Book a licensed mountain guide in advance; the price usually includes all safety equipment.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text: If you only want the views without the climb, Le Pouce next door offers a similar panorama on a straightforward trail.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text: The hills around Port Louis give runners in and near the capital steep training without a long drive. The city sits in a bowl under the Moka Range, so climbing starts almost from the streets.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text: Signal Mountain, with the Marie Reine de la Paix area on its slopes, is one of the more runnable climbs close to the city centre and works well for hill repeats.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text: The trail along the Canal Anglais, an old canal path, leads up towards the plateau and suits steady uphill runs. The Pouce valley, below Le Pouce, offers longer and more challenging trails that link the city to the mountains.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text: Runners who work in Port Louis and want hill sessions before or after work, and hikers preparing for bigger mountains such as Le Pouce, Pieter Both or Le Morne.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text: Port Louis is one of the hottest places on the island because it is sheltered from the trade winds. Train at first light or in the evening, and carry water even on short sessions.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text: Paths near the city are well used but vary in quality. Run with others when exploring the trails in the Pouce valley for the first time.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: The austral winter, from May to November, is the best period for hiking and running in Mauritius: it is cooler and drier, and trails are less muddy.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: The summer months, roughly November to April, are hot and humid with heavy rain, and cyclones can affect the island.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: During summer, train at dawn, shorten long efforts and stay off mountain trails after heavy rain, when rock and mud become dangerous. Always check weather warnings before heading into the mountains.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text:
Always check weather warnings before heading into the mountains.
The Royal Raid has been held since 2006 and is the island's longest-running trail race.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: It takes place in the Black River Gorges, with distances such as 15 km, 37 km and 70 km offered in past editions. It also opens the Mauritius Odyssey, a multi-stage event.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text:
It also opens the Mauritius Odyssey, a multi-stage event.
The Dodo Trail, held in July, is the island's signature trail race. The 2026 edition gathered more than 3,000 runners.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: The 2026 edition gathered more than 3,000 runners. Its flagship Xtreme course covers about 50 km with around 3,500 m of ascent, starting at dawn in the Le Morne area and finishing in Tamarin.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: Shorter formats include the Trooper 25 km, the Venture 10 km and the Rookie 5 km.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: A typical approach on the island combines the training grounds in this guide: easy laps at Trou aux Cerfs or on the coast, hill strength on La Tourelle de Tamarin or the Port Louis hills, and race-specific long runs in the Black River Gorges.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: Race dates and formats change each year, so confirm them with the organisers before planning.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text: Tamarind Falls, also called the Seven Cascades or Sept Cascades, is a chain of waterfalls in a forested canyon on the central plateau, near Henrietta in the Vacoas area.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text:
It is the island's classic waterfall hike, with natural pools for a swim along the way.
Most guided groups meet at Henrietta, often at the bus station, and walk into the canyon from there.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text: Half-day hikes of about three hours visit some of the falls; longer full-day itineraries reach more of them. Itineraries vary, and operators quote different numbers of waterfalls, so check what is included before booking.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text: The hike is moderate, with slippery rocks, river crossings and muddy sections.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text: The route is not waymarked and side paths multiply through the canyon, which is why local guides recommend a guide here more firmly than on any other hike, even though one is not compulsory.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text: Avoid the canyon during and after heavy rain, when river levels rise quickly and the rocks are treacherous. The drier months from May to November are safest.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text:
The drier months from May to November are safest.
Wear hiking shoes with good grip that can get wet, and bring a windproof layer, swimwear and water.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text: Swimming and jumping into pools should only be done where a guide confirms it is safe.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text: Trou aux Cerfs is a dormant volcanic crater in Curepipe, on the central plateau. The crater is roughly 300 to 350 m across and about 80 m deep, and a road around its rim is closed to traffic.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
It is one of the most popular places in Mauritius to jog or walk.
The rim road is paved, wide and fairly flat, and one lap is about 1 to 1.2 km.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text: That makes it ideal for easy runs, steady tempo efforts and lap-based intervals, because every lap is the same distance and there are no cars.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text: Walkers, families and runners share the loop, especially early in the morning and in the late afternoon. Viewpoints around the rim look into the crater and, on clear days, across to the mountains of the west and the Moka Range.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text: Beginners building up to their first continuous run, runners doing recovery or tempo sessions, and anyone who wants a safe, measured loop without traffic.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text: It is too flat for hill training; for that, use the mountains or La Tourelle de Tamarin.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
Curepipe is higher, cooler and wetter than the coast, so it is a good place to train in the hot months, but expect drizzle and mist. Some viewpoints have uneven natural surfaces.
Access is free.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
Some viewpoints have uneven natural surfaces.
Access is free. Combine laps here with longer runs on the plateau roads if you need more distance.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text:
For interval sessions and speed work, nothing replaces a measured track. The main athletics venues in Mauritius are the Maryse Justin Stadium in Réduit and the Stade Germain Comarmond in Bambous.
The stadium is named after Maryse Justin-Pyndiah, a Mauritian long-distance runner who specialised in the marathon. It is used by the Mauritius Athletics Association and hosts national championships.
In the west, near Bambous, this stadium is used mostly for football and athletics, and has also hosted national youth athletics championships.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text:
In the west, near Bambous, this stadium is used mostly for football and athletics, and has also hosted national youth athletics championships.
Public opening hours and fees for casual runners are not published by the athletics association, whose calendars list competitions and club training. The reliable way to train on a track is to join an athletics club or to ask the Mauritius Athletics Association or the stadium administration about access.
Runners doing structured speed work, such as 400 m repeats or tempo intervals, and anyone preparing for road races who wants precise pacing.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text: Runners doing structured speed work, such as 400 m repeats or tempo intervals, and anyone preparing for road races who wants precise pacing. For an open-access measured loop without traffic, the Trou aux Cerfs crater rim in Curepipe is the usual alternative.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Black River Gorges National Park protects the largest area of native forest left in Mauritius, in the south-west of the island. It is home to rare endemic birds such as the echo parakeet, the pink pigeon and the Mauritius kestrel. Entry to the park and its trails is free.
There are two official entrances with visitor centres: Pétrin, on the plateau, and Rivière Noire, at the bottom of the gorges on the west side. Rangers there can advise on current trail conditions, and trail maps are available. Some sources say the park gates close at about 5 pm.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Rangers there can advise on current trail conditions, and trail maps are available. Some sources say the park gates close at about 5 pm.
The Macchabée forest loop starts from Pétrin and runs through some of the best native forest on the island. Its length varies by variant, with sources quoting anywhere from about 8 to 14 km. The Parakeet Trail is a much harder one-way descent of roughly 6 to 8 km through steep, technical terrain, taking most people three to four hours.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Gentler options include short walks to viewpoints such as Alexandra Falls and the Black River Gorges viewpoint.
Difficulty ranges from easy viewpoint strolls to hard, technical descents. Trails are not always well marked, so check the route and conditions at a visitor centre before you set off.
May to November is the best season, with fewer muddy paths. The plateau is often misty and cooler than the coast, so bring a light rain jacket.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:
Black River Peak, Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire, is the highest point in Mauritius at about 828 m. It stands inside Black River Gorges National Park, and despite being the highest summit it is one of the shortest hikes to a major peak on the island.
The usual trailhead is on the B103 Plaine Champagne road, close to the Black River Gorges viewpoint. Parking at the trailhead fits only two or three cars, so many hikers leave the car at the viewpoint car park a short walk away.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:
Parking at the trailhead fits only two or three cars, so many hikers leave the car at the viewpoint car park a short walk away. From the viewpoint side the return hike is about 3 to 3.5 km with under 200 m of climbing, and most people reach the top in about an hour to an hour and a half.
The trail is mostly well maintained and easy to follow through native forest. The final section is steeper and rockier, and ropes help on the rock in places.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:
The final section is steeper and rockier, and ropes help on the rock in places. The trailhead is not well signposted, so check a map before you go. From the summit you look down over the west coast, Tamarin bay and Le Morne.
May to November is drier and less muddy. Start in the morning, and turn back if the summit is in cloud and the rock is wet.
Entry to the national park is free and no permit is required. Guided hikes are available if you prefer not to navigate the unsigned start.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text: Entry to the national park is free and no permit is required. Guided hikes are available if you prefer not to navigate the unsigned start. Bring a light jacket: Plaine Champagne is noticeably cooler and windier than the coast.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text:
Bras d'Eau National Park is a coastal forest park in the north-east of Mauritius. Its trails run through forest that includes mangroves and endemic trees, and they are much flatter than the mountain trails of the west and centre.
Bras d'Eau is a good place for fairly easy trail running. Trails start from the visitor centre, and the gentle terrain makes it a natural first step from road running to trail running, or a place for relaxed long runs on soft ground.

chunks.title: Bras d'Eau National Park
chunks.text:
Beginners trying trail running for the first time, runners in the east and north of the island, and anyone who wants shaded, quiet running away from traffic without technical terrain.
Being on the coast, it is warm and humid; the forest gives more shade than beach routes. After heavy rain, parts of the trails can be muddy.
Pick up information at the visitor centre before heading out, and stay on the marked trails to protect the forest.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text:
When the goal is easy mileage, recovery runs or speed on the flat, the coast is the place to train. Each side of the island has its own classic route.
Flic en Flac has about 8 km of white-sand beach and a flat seafront road, which makes it one of the best places on the island for beginners and for early-morning runs. Running on sand also builds strength in the feet and calves.
Belle Mare has a beachfront path and roughly 1.5 km of firm sand road along the beach, with quiet farm roads inland for longer runs.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
sections: North: Mont Choisy and Grand Baie
chunks.text:
Belle Mare has a beachfront path and roughly 1.5 km of firm sand road along the beach, with quiet farm roads inland for longer runs. One mapped beachfront loop from Belle Mare is about 10 km.
The coastal road leading to Mont Choisy beach is quieter than the main roads. Sections of the B13 through Pereybère, Grand Baie and Mont Choisy have a narrow sidewalk or shoulder, so run there with care and at quiet times.
A flat trail runs along the water at Le Morne, a scenic option for an easy run before or after hiking the mountain.

chunks.title: Flat coastal runs
chunks.text:
A flat trail runs along the water at Le Morne, a scenic option for an easy run before or after hiking the mountain.
The coast is hot and humid for most of the year. Run at dawn or late in the day, carry water, and wear shoes on rocky beaches where sea urchins hide.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text:
Corps de Garde is a mountain of about 720 m that towers over Rose Hill, Beau Bassin and Quatre Bornes. From its ridge you see the whole central plateau, the west coast and, on clear days, Port Louis.
The classic route is a loop above Rose Hill. One detailed guide describes it as about 7 km with more than 600 m of ascent, and other sources give 2 to 4 hours. The path is marked with white stones up to the ridge.
It is not really a beginner hike.

chunks.title: Corps de Garde
chunks.text:
The path is marked with white stones up to the ridge.
It is not really a beginner hike. The climb starts steeply, with rocky steps where you need your hands, and the slopes near the summit are challenging. Sources rate it medium to hard.
The route has very little shade, so avoid the middle of the day. May to November is cooler; in summer, go at first light.
It is free and no guide is needed. Take about two litres of water per person, sun protection and shoes with good grip.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text:

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text:
Long runs on the forest loops build endurance, and the climbs out of the gorges build strength for steep ascents and technical descents. The Royal Raid, the island's longest-running trail race, held since 2006, takes place in the Black River Gorges, with distances such as 15 km, 37 km and 70 km offered in past editions. Training on its trails is the most race-specific preparation you can do on the island.
Intermediate and experienced trail runners preparing for the Royal Raid, the Dodo Trail or races abroad.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges for trail running
chunks.text:
Intermediate and experienced trail runners preparing for the Royal Raid, the Dodo Trail or races abroad. Beginners should start on the shorter, well-used trails from the Pétrin visitor centre and run with someone who knows the network.
Footing gets very muddy and slippery in the wet season. The austral winter, from May to November, is the best period for long runs. Trails are not always well marked, and there is little phone signal in places.
Entry is free. Check routes with rangers at the visitor centres, carry water and a map, and tell someone your planned route.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text:
La Tourelle de Tamarin is a steep mountain less than a kilometre from the coast at Tamarin, on the west of the island. Runners use it as a brutal hill-training ground: about 560 m of ascent over roughly 4.4 km return.

Fixed ropes equip some of the steps, so expect to use your hands. The descent is as important to practise as the climb: take it carefully, especially when tired.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text:
The descent is as important to practise as the climb: take it carefully, especially when tired.
Trail runners and hikers preparing for races with a lot of climbing, such as the Dodo Trail or the Royal Raid. It is not a beginner route; build up on easier hills first, such as Le Pouce or the Port Louis hills.
The west coast is hot and dry, and the slope offers little shade. Train at dawn or late in the afternoon.

chunks.title: La Tourelle de Tamarin
chunks.text:
The west coast is hot and dry, and the slope offers little shade. Train at dawn or late in the afternoon. Darkness falls quickly in Mauritius, in about twenty minutes, between about 5:45 pm and 7 pm depending on the season, so carry a headlamp on evening sessions.
Bring plenty of water and gloves for the rope sections. Avoid it after rain, when the steps become slippery.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text:
Le Morne Brabant is the 556 m basalt mountain on the south-western peninsula of Mauritius. It is a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, inscribed in 2008, because its cliffs sheltered escaped enslaved people, the maroons, in the 18th and 19th centuries. Hike it with that history in mind.
The trail starts at a gate near the base of the mountain, where hikers sign in and out of a register for safety. The lower trail climbs to a viewpoint with a large cross, with views over the lagoon and the south-west coast.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text:
The lower trail climbs to a viewpoint with a large cross, with views over the lagoon and the south-west coast. Above the cross, the final section to the summit is a steep scramble where you climb on all fours. A full return to the summit takes about 3 to 5 hours.
Published opening hours differ between sources, but the gate opens early in the morning and late starts are not allowed, with the last departure in the early afternoon. Access is closed on rainy days. Sources also disagree on whether a licensed guide is required above the cross.

chunks.title: Le Morne Brabant
chunks.difficulty: Moderate to the cross, hard to the summit
chunks.text:
Access is closed on rainy days. Sources also disagree on whether a licensed guide is required above the cross. Check the current rules on site or with a local operator before you plan the summit.
To the cross, the hike is moderate but hot. The summit section is hard and exposed, and should be skipped after rain because the rock becomes slippery.
Start at dawn. There is very little shade, and the south-west coast gets hot by mid-morning. The cooler months from May to November are the most pleasant.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text:
Le Pouce, "the thumb", is the third-highest mountain in Mauritius at about 812 m. Its thumb-shaped summit rises from the Moka Range directly above Port Louis, and it is one of the most popular half-day hikes on the island because it is short, well trodden and close to the capital.
The best-known trailhead is the village of Petit Verger, near Saint Pierre, where a well-marked path climbs through sugar cane fields and patches of forest. Other approaches start from the Moka side and from the Tranquebar side of Port Louis.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text:
Other approaches start from the Moka side and from the Tranquebar side of Port Louis. A common return route is about 4 to 5 km, and most walkers take 2 to 4 hours depending on the starting point and their pace.
The hike is easy to moderate for most of the way. The last few hundred metres to the summit are steep and rocky, and you need good balance and sometimes your hands. The reward is a 360° view over Port Louis, the northern plains and the neighbouring peak of Pieter Both.

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text:
The reward is a 360° view over Port Louis, the northern plains and the neighbouring peak of Pieter Both.
The drier, cooler months from May to November are the most comfortable. Start early in the morning: the path has stretches without shade. After heavy rain the upper rock section becomes slippery.
No permit or guide is needed. Carry at least a litre and a half of water, a hat and shoes with good grip. Guided sunrise and sunset hikes are also offered by local operators.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
Lion Mountain, Montagne du Lion, rises to about 480 m above Vieux Grand Port, near Mahébourg on the south-east coast. Seen from the coast road, its ridge looks like a resting lion. It is the best-known hike in the east of the island.
The trail starts in Vieux Grand Port, near the police station, and crosses sugar cane fields before climbing the lion's spine. The return hike is about 4.5 to 5 km and usually takes 2 to 3 hours. From the top you look over the bay of Grand Port, the lagoon and the islets offshore.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
From the top you look over the bay of Grand Port, the lagoon and the islets offshore.
Sources rate it moderate to hard. The first part of the climb follows a rocky spine where you use your hands as well as your legs, with a few easy but airy scrambling moves. Waymarking is limited to paint marks and ribbons, so a guide is advisable if you do not know the route.
Hike it in dry weather only, in any season. The rock becomes dangerous when wet.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
Hike it in dry weather only, in any season. The rock becomes dangerous when wet. There is no water on the route and little shade, so an early morning start is best.
Carry all your water. Guided hikes with local guides are offered from Mahébourg and the surrounding area.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text:
Pieter Both is the second-highest mountain in Mauritius, at about 820 m, in the Moka Range above Port Louis. It is instantly recognisable by the round boulder, the "head", balanced on top of its narrow summit spire.
A hiking path through forest and grassland leads to the shoulder below the head. The final section, up the head itself, is a rock climb rather than a hike. Guides use fixed ropes and metal rungs bolted into the basalt, and supply helmets, harnesses and ropes after a safety briefing. Allow a full day with a guided group.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text:
Allow a full day with a guided group.
This is the hardest summit in this collection. Local guides describe it as the only Mauritian ascent that genuinely requires guiding, and hikers who have done it warn that it is dangerous without a guide. A head for heights is essential, and it is not suitable for beginners.
Climb only in dry, calm weather, from May to November if possible. Wind and wet rock make the summit block unsafe, and guides cancel when conditions are poor.
Book a licensed mountain guide in advance; the price usually includes all safety equipment.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text: Book a licensed mountain guide in advance; the price usually includes all safety equipment. If you only want the views without the climb, Le Pouce next door offers a similar panorama on a straightforward trail.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text:
The hills around Port Louis give runners in and near the capital steep training without a long drive. The city sits in a bowl under the Moka Range, so climbing starts almost from the streets.
Signal Mountain, with the Marie Reine de la Paix area on its slopes, is one of the more runnable climbs close to the city centre and works well for hill repeats. The trail along the Canal Anglais, an old canal path, leads up towards the plateau and suits steady uphill runs.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text:
The trail along the Canal Anglais, an old canal path, leads up towards the plateau and suits steady uphill runs. The Pouce valley, below Le Pouce, offers longer and more challenging trails that link the city to the mountains.
Runners who work in Port Louis and want hill sessions before or after work, and hikers preparing for bigger mountains such as Le Pouce, Pieter Both or Le Morne.
Port Louis is one of the hottest places on the island because it is sheltered from the trade winds.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text:
Port Louis is one of the hottest places on the island because it is sheltered from the trade winds. Train at first light or in the evening, and carry water even on short sessions.
Paths near the city are well used but vary in quality. Run with others when exploring the trails in the Pouce valley for the first time.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text:
The austral winter, from May to November, is the best period for hiking and running in Mauritius: it is cooler and drier, and trails are less muddy. The summer months, roughly November to April, are hot and humid with heavy rain, and cyclones can affect the island. During summer, train at dawn, shorten long efforts and stay off mountain trails after heavy rain, when rock and mud become dangerous. Always check weather warnings before heading into the mountains.
The Royal Raid has been held since 2006 and is the island's longest-running trail race.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text:
Always check weather warnings before heading into the mountains.
The Royal Raid has been held since 2006 and is the island's longest-running trail race. It takes place in the Black River Gorges, with distances such as 15 km, 37 km and 70 km offered in past editions. It also opens the Mauritius Odyssey, a multi-stage event.
The Dodo Trail, held in July, is the island's signature trail race. The 2026 edition gathered more than 3,000 runners.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text: The Dodo Trail, held in July, is the island's signature trail race. The 2026 edition gathered more than 3,000 runners. Its flagship Xtreme course covers about 50 km with around 3,500 m of ascent, starting at dawn in the Le Morne area and finishing in Tamarin. Shorter formats include the Trooper 25 km, the Venture 10 km and the Rookie 5 km.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text:
Shorter formats include the Trooper 25 km, the Venture 10 km and the Rookie 5 km.
A typical approach on the island combines the training grounds in this guide: easy laps at Trou aux Cerfs or on the coast, hill strength on La Tourelle de Tamarin or the Port Louis hills, and race-specific long runs in the Black River Gorges. Race dates and formats change each year, so confirm them with the organisers before planning.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text:
Tamarind Falls, also called the Seven Cascades or Sept Cascades, is a chain of waterfalls in a forested canyon on the central plateau, near Henrietta in the Vacoas area. It is the island's classic waterfall hike, with natural pools for a swim along the way.
Most guided groups meet at Henrietta, often at the bus station, and walk into the canyon from there. Half-day hikes of about three hours visit some of the falls; longer full-day itineraries reach more of them. Itineraries vary, and operators quote different numbers of waterfalls, so check what is included before booking.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text:
Itineraries vary, and operators quote different numbers of waterfalls, so check what is included before booking.
The hike is moderate, with slippery rocks, river crossings and muddy sections. The route is not waymarked and side paths multiply through the canyon, which is why local guides recommend a guide here more firmly than on any other hike, even though one is not compulsory.
Avoid the canyon during and after heavy rain, when river levels rise quickly and the rocks are treacherous. The drier months from May to November are safest.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text:
The drier months from May to November are safest.
Wear hiking shoes with good grip that can get wet, and bring a windproof layer, swimwear and water. Swimming and jumping into pools should only be done where a guide confirms it is safe.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
Trou aux Cerfs is a dormant volcanic crater in Curepipe, on the central plateau. The crater is roughly 300 to 350 m across and about 80 m deep, and a road around its rim is closed to traffic. It is one of the most popular places in Mauritius to jog or walk.
The rim road is paved, wide and fairly flat, and one lap is about 1 to 1.2 km. That makes it ideal for easy runs, steady tempo efforts and lap-based intervals, because every lap is the same distance and there are no cars.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
That makes it ideal for easy runs, steady tempo efforts and lap-based intervals, because every lap is the same distance and there are no cars. Walkers, families and runners share the loop, especially early in the morning and in the late afternoon. Viewpoints around the rim look into the crater and, on clear days, across to the mountains of the west and the Moka Range.
Beginners building up to their first continuous run, runners doing recovery or tempo sessions, and anyone who wants a safe, measured loop without traffic.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
Beginners building up to their first continuous run, runners doing recovery or tempo sessions, and anyone who wants a safe, measured loop without traffic. It is too flat for hill training; for that, use the mountains or La Tourelle de Tamarin.
Curepipe is higher, cooler and wetter than the coast, so it is a good place to train in the hot months, but expect drizzle and mist. Some viewpoints have uneven natural surfaces.
Access is free. Combine laps here with longer runs on the plateau roads if you need more distance.

chunks.title: Athletics tracks
chunks.text:
For interval sessions and speed work, nothing replaces a measured track. The main athletics venues in Mauritius are the Maryse Justin Stadium in Réduit and the Stade Germain Comarmond in Bambous.
The stadium is named after Maryse Justin-Pyndiah, a Mauritian long-distance runner who specialised in the marathon. It is used by the Mauritius Athletics Association and hosts national championships.
In the west, near Bambous, this stadium is used mostly for football and athletics, and has also hosted national youth athletics championships.
Public opening hours and fees for casual runners are not published by the athletics association, whose calendars list competitions and club training. The reliable way to train on a track is to join an athletics club or to ask the Mauritius Athletics Association or the stadium administration about access.
Runners doing structured speed work, such as 400 m repeats or tempo intervals, and anyone preparing for road races who wants precise pacing. For an open-access measured loop without traffic, the Trou aux Cerfs crater rim in Curepipe is the usual alternative.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Black River Gorges National Park protects the largest area of native forest left in Mauritius, in the south-west of the island. It is home to rare endemic birds such as the echo parakeet, the pink pigeon and the Mauritius kestrel. Entry to the park and its trails is free.
There are two official entrances with visitor centres: Pétrin, on the plateau, and Rivière Noire, at the bottom of the gorges on the west side. Rangers there can advise on current trail conditions, and trail maps are available. Some sources say the park gates close at about 5 pm.
The Macchabée forest loop starts from Pétrin and runs through some of the best native forest on the island. Its length varies by variant, with sources quoting anywhere from about 8 to 14 km. The Parakeet Trail is a much harder one-way descent of roughly 6 to 8 km through steep, technical terrain, taking most people three to four hours. Gentler options include short walks to viewpoints such as Alexandra Falls and the Black River Gorges viewpoint.
Difficulty ranges from easy viewpoint strolls to hard, technical descents. Trails are not always well marked, so check the route and conditions at a visitor centre before you set off.
May to November is the best season, with fewer muddy paths.

chunks.title: Black River Gorges National Park trails
chunks.text:
Difficulty ranges from easy viewpoint strolls to hard, technical descents. Trails are not always well marked, so check the route and conditions at a visitor centre before you set off.
May to November is the best season, with fewer muddy paths. The plateau is often misty and cooler than the coast, so bring a light rain jacket.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:
Black River Peak, Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire, is the highest point in Mauritius at about 828 m. It stands inside Black River Gorges National Park, and despite being the highest summit it is one of the shortest hikes to a major peak on the island.
The usual trailhead is on the B103 Plaine Champagne road, close to the Black River Gorges viewpoint. Parking at the trailhead fits only two or three cars, so many hikers leave the car at the viewpoint car park a short walk away. From the viewpoint side the return hike is about 3 to 3.5 km with under 200 m of climbing, and most people reach the top in about an hour to an hour and a half.
The trail is mostly well maintained and easy to follow through native forest. The final section is steeper and rockier, and ropes help on the rock in places. The trailhead is not well signposted, so check a map before you go. From the summit you look down over the west coast, Tamarin bay and Le Morne.
May to November is drier and less muddy. Start in the morning, and turn back if the summit is in cloud and the rock is wet.
Entry to the national park is free and no permit is required.

chunks.title: Black River Peak
chunks.text:

chunks.title: Le Pouce
chunks.text:
The drier, cooler months from May to November are the most comfortable. Start early in the morning: the path has stretches without shade. After heavy rain the upper rock section becomes slippery.
No permit or guide is needed. Carry at least a litre and a half of water, a hat and shoes with good grip. Guided sunrise and sunset hikes are also offered by local operators.

chunks.title: Lion Mountain
chunks.text:
Lion Mountain, Montagne du Lion, rises to about 480 m above Vieux Grand Port, near Mahébourg on the south-east coast. Seen from the coast road, its ridge looks like a resting lion. It is the best-known hike in the east of the island.
The trail starts in Vieux Grand Port, near the police station, and crosses sugar cane fields before climbing the lion's spine. The return hike is about 4.5 to 5 km and usually takes 2 to 3 hours. From the top you look over the bay of Grand Port, the lagoon and the islets offshore.
Sources rate it moderate to hard. The first part of the climb follows a rocky spine where you use your hands as well as your legs, with a few easy but airy scrambling moves. Waymarking is limited to paint marks and ribbons, so a guide is advisable if you do not know the route.
Hike it in dry weather only, in any season. The rock becomes dangerous when wet. There is no water on the route and little shade, so an early morning start is best.
Carry all your water. Guided hikes with local guides are offered from Mahébourg and the surrounding area.

chunks.title: Pieter Both
chunks.text:
Pieter Both is the second-highest mountain in Mauritius, at about 820 m, in the Moka Range above Port Louis. It is instantly recognisable by the round boulder, the "head", balanced on top of its narrow summit spire.
A hiking path through forest and grassland leads to the shoulder below the head. The final section, up the head itself, is a rock climb rather than a hike. Guides use fixed ropes and metal rungs bolted into the basalt, and supply helmets, harnesses and ropes after a safety briefing. Allow a full day with a guided group.
This is the hardest summit in this collection. Local guides describe it as the only Mauritian ascent that genuinely requires guiding, and hikers who have done it warn that it is dangerous without a guide. A head for heights is essential, and it is not suitable for beginners.
Climb only in dry, calm weather, from May to November if possible. Wind and wet rock make the summit block unsafe, and guides cancel when conditions are poor.
Book a licensed mountain guide in advance; the price usually includes all safety equipment. If you only want the views without the climb, Le Pouce next door offers a similar panorama on a straightforward trail.

chunks.title: Port Louis hills
chunks.text:
The hills around Port Louis give runners in and near the capital steep training without a long drive. The city sits in a bowl under the Moka Range, so climbing starts almost from the streets.
Signal Mountain, with the Marie Reine de la Paix area on its slopes, is one of the more runnable climbs close to the city centre and works well for hill repeats. The trail along the Canal Anglais, an old canal path, leads up towards the plateau and suits steady uphill runs. The Pouce valley, below Le Pouce, offers longer and more challenging trails that link the city to the mountains.
Runners who work in Port Louis and want hill sessions before or after work, and hikers preparing for bigger mountains such as Le Pouce, Pieter Both or Le Morne.
Port Louis is one of the hottest places on the island because it is sheltered from the trade winds. Train at first light or in the evening, and carry water even on short sessions.
Paths near the city are well used but vary in quality. Run with others when exploring the trails in the Pouce valley for the first time.

chunks.title: Training seasons and trail races
chunks.text:
The austral winter, from May to November, is the best period for hiking and running in Mauritius: it is cooler and drier, and trails are less muddy. The summer months, roughly November to April, are hot and humid with heavy rain, and cyclones can affect the island. During summer, train at dawn, shorten long efforts and stay off mountain trails after heavy rain, when rock and mud become dangerous. Always check weather warnings before heading into the mountains.
The Royal Raid has been held since 2006 and is the island's longest-running trail race. It takes place in the Black River Gorges, with distances such as 15 km, 37 km and 70 km offered in past editions. It also opens the Mauritius Odyssey, a multi-stage event.
The Dodo Trail, held in July, is the island's signature trail race. The 2026 edition gathered more than 3,000 runners. Its flagship Xtreme course covers about 50 km with around 3,500 m of ascent, starting at dawn in the Le Morne area and finishing in Tamarin. Shorter formats include the Trooper 25 km, the Venture 10 km and the Rookie 5 km.

chunks.text:

A typical approach on the island combines the training grounds in this guide: easy laps at Trou aux Cerfs or on the coast, hill strength on La Tourelle de Tamarin or the Port Louis hills, and race-specific long runs in the Black River Gorges. Race dates and formats change each year, so confirm them with the organisers before planning.

chunks.title: Tamarind Falls (Seven Cascades)
chunks.text:
Tamarind Falls, also called the Seven Cascades or Sept Cascades, is a chain of waterfalls in a forested canyon on the central plateau, near Henrietta in the Vacoas area. It is the island's classic waterfall hike, with natural pools for a swim along the way.
Most guided groups meet at Henrietta, often at the bus station, and walk into the canyon from there. Half-day hikes of about three hours visit some of the falls; longer full-day itineraries reach more of them. Itineraries vary, and operators quote different numbers of waterfalls, so check what is included before booking.
The hike is moderate, with slippery rocks, river crossings and muddy sections. The route is not waymarked and side paths multiply through the canyon, which is why local guides recommend a guide here more firmly than on any other hike, even though one is not compulsory.
Avoid the canyon during and after heavy rain, when river levels rise quickly and the rocks are treacherous. The drier months from May to November are safest.
Wear hiking shoes with good grip that can get wet, and bring a windproof layer, swimwear and water. Swimming and jumping into pools should only be done where a guide confirms it is safe.

chunks.title: Trou aux Cerfs crater loop
chunks.text:
Trou aux Cerfs is a dormant volcanic crater in Curepipe, on the central plateau. The crater is roughly 300 to 350 m across and about 80 m deep, and a road around its rim is closed to traffic. It is one of the most popular places in Mauritius to jog or walk.
The rim road is paved, wide and fairly flat, and one lap is about 1 to 1.2 km. That makes it ideal for easy runs, steady tempo efforts and lap-based intervals, because every lap is the same distance and there are no cars. Walkers, families and runners share the loop, especially early in the morning and in the late afternoon. Viewpoints around the rim look into the crater and, on clear days, across to the mountains of the west and the Moka Range.
Beginners building up to their first continuous run, runners doing recovery or tempo sessions, and anyone who wants a safe, measured loop without traffic. It is too flat for hill training; for that, use the mountains or La Tourelle de Tamarin.
Curepipe is higher, cooler and wetter than the coast, so it is a good place to train in the hot months, but expect drizzle and mist. Some viewpoints have uneven natural surfaces.
Access is free.
